window: Papers published since 30 Sep 2026 (plus one strong August item missed earlier)
note: Summaries are written by Claude from each paper's abstract. Items marked 'title only' had no abstract available — open the paper before relying on them. Dates given as YYYY-MM have no exact day available.

items.title: Penetration of a sphere in a pool: Secondary pinch-off
items.authors: P. K. Billa, C. Tropea, P. S. Mahapatra et al.

summary.problem: After a sphere enters water its air cavity can pinch off more than once, and these later pinch-offs decide whether a light sphere rises back up or keeps sinking; wettability matters but past work stopped at the first pinch-off.
summary.method: High-speed imaging (1000–2000 fps) of 4, 6 and 10 mm hydrophobic (~100°) and superhydrophobic (~155°) spheres dropped into a deep tank, with tracked trajectories and a gravity–buoyancy–drag force balance.
summary.result: Over impact speeds of 0.89–3.52 m/s (Fr 2.8–17.8), no sphere with density ratio ≥ 3.26 or contact angle below 97° came back up; superhydrophobic 4 and 6 mm spheres did, and hydrophobic ones only in some repeats.

items.why: A fresh experimental dataset where the outcome hinges on contact angle on a moving sphere — exactly requirement 4 of your proposal — and a ready validation case for your water-entry runs past the first pinch-off. Note the 155° angle was measured on a flat plate, not on the sphere.

items.title: Quantum-Classical Iterative Refinement for the Pressure-Poisson Equation on NISQ Hardware
items.authors: D. Ahn, B. Park, R. S. Myong et al.

summary.problem: A single quantum linear solve of the projection-method pressure equation leaves an error floor on noisy hardware; earlier schemes needed state infidelity below 1e-7.
summary.method: Repeatedly solve for the normalized residual on a MAC grid and scale each quantum direction by a least-squares fit to the physical residual, so quantum error only slows contraction instead of setting a floor.
summary.result: On IBM hardware (16×16, 4 qubits) the relative residual fell below 1e-7 in 8–10 corrections in all 20 runs, versus 0.33–0.59 for a single solve; a 64×64 pilot needed 13 corrections and IonQ Forte reached 5.6e-8 in nine.

items.why: The most practical answer yet to the noise floor your quantum pressure-solver study has to confront; iterative refinement also sidesteps part of the conditioning problem in your Poisson condition-number note, though it was shown only for constant density.

items.title: Investigation on splash and airflow evolution mechanism during water-entry of a hydrophobic sphere

summary.method: From the title: a study of how the splash and the air flow into the cavity develop when a hydrophobic sphere enters water.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Directly on topic 1. The airflow into the cavity connects to the air film in your solver, so check whether it reports gas speeds you could compare against.

items.authors: L. M. Piskol, T. Grahs, S. Langer

summary.method: The Jacobi iteration is written as a polynomial of a block-encoded operator using quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), and tested on 1D and 2D Poisson problems — including the pressure Poisson equation inside Chorin's projection method for lid-driven cavity flow.
summary.problem: Most quantum linear solvers try to invert the matrix directly, while CFD codes rely on iterative methods such as Jacobi.
summary.result: The number of ancilla qubits stays constant as iterations increase; circuit depth grows linearly with the number of Jacobi iterations.

items.title: A QSVT-Based Quantum Jacobi Algorithm for Linear Systems with Application to the Poisson Equation
items.why: The closest paper to your quantum pressure-solver study: it uses exactly Chorin's projection step. Compare its iteration-count argument with your condition-number numbers — Jacobi needs O(κ) iterations, so your multiphase κ would make the circuit very deep.

items.authors: X. Chen, X. Li, B. Yin et al.

summary.method: A coupled VOF/level-set method combined with an immersed boundary method and discrete element method, extended to an axisymmetric configuration.
summary.problem: How does a particle striking a wall-attached bubble make it detach?
summary.result: Three detachment modes are identified: capillary-wave, bubble-rebound and particle-rebound.

items.title: Bubble detachment from solid surfaces induced by impacting particles
items.why: Combines the three ingredients of your thesis — VOF interface, immersed solid, and a wall-attached interface — in a JFM paper. Check how they treat the contact angle on the wall while the particle moves.

items.title: A Variational Quantum Linear Solver via Block Encoding for the Poisson Equation
items.authors: V. Dsouza, A. Singhal, A. Khan et al.

summary.problem: VQLS for the discrete Poisson equation is expensive because LCU-based cost functions need O(L²) circuits per evaluation.
summary.method: Uses an exact block encoding of the discrete Laplacian so each cost evaluation needs one circuit, tested on sinusoidal forcing, a Gaussian-source heat problem and the lid-driven-cavity pressure-Poisson equation (Neumann boundaries).
summary.result: The abstract gives no numbers; it reports the single-circuit cost and that the choice of classical optimizer strongly changes where training stalls.

items.why: Older than this window but missed by earlier feeds: a VQLS baseline that includes a Neumann pressure-Poisson case, useful as a comparison point beside HHL and QSVT in your quantum pressure-solver study.

items.title: Coupled Rigid-Body Motion and Binary Phase Change: A Sharp Level-Set/Embedded-Boundary Method
items.authors: C.-F. Zhang, Z.-H. Xue, J. Zhang et al.

summary.problem: Freely moving solids that also melt are hard to simulate because fluid forces move the body while melting changes its shape at the same interface.
summary.method: Level-set tracking of a solid that translates, rotates and melts on a fixed Cartesian grid, embedded-boundary conditions at the surface, conservative moving cut cells for liquid heat and salt, and sub-iteration of loads, motion and phase change each step.
summary.result: Matches reference solutions in rigid-body and melting tests, gives a Strouhal number of 0.1175 against 0.1172 from a body-fitted solver for a settling oblate ellipsoid, and simulates a 3D ellipsoid that moves and melts at once.

items.why: A recent example of a solid moving without remeshing plus conservative cut-cell transport (requirements 1 and 2), with a coupling loop you can compare with Pathak & Raessi; the authors admit the level-set volume error (~1e-2) is worse than VOF.

items.why: Relevant to your earlier FSI-coupling study: explicit partitioned schemes usually suffer from the added-mass instability. Robin–Robin coupling is one of the standard cures.

items.title: Dynamics of singular-jet formation during the collapse of drop-impact craters

summary.problem: Why some collapsing drop-impact craters produce very thin, very fast singular jets.
summary.method: 2D axisymmetric direct simulations in Basilisk with adaptive mesh refinement, checked against experiments.
summary.result: For a 3.64 mm drop the singular jet reaches 61.7 m/s with a ~210 μm trapped bubble and a critical wall-to-base angle of 109.2°; for We 100–200 and Fr 45–92 the bubble-entrainment band lies between We = 45.5 Fr^0.237 and We = 53.5 Fr^0.251.

items.why: Cavity collapse and jetting are the same physics as the Worthington jet after water entry; a good stress test for curvature and spurious currents in your PLIC code at high interface speeds.

items.title: Amortized Transport-Map Likelihoods for Hierarchical Inverse Problems with Application to Wetting

summary.problem: Bayesian inference of wetting properties needs one forward simulation per group for each posterior evaluation, which is very costly.
summary.method: Train a triangular transport-map likelihood once per experimental design and reuse it, inferring wetting parameters from photos of a stable hole in a thin liquid film.
summary.result: Posteriors match direct sampling at the validation design, with several hundred times fewer forward solves per posterior and about five orders of magnitude fewer across 200 posteriors; agreement is weaker at a larger-scale design.

items.why: A rigorous way to infer contact-angle parameters from images with uncertainty, which could set the static and dynamic angles in your three-phase contact-line cases instead of hand-tuning them.

items.title: Some analytical solutions for the evaporative flux and the flow inside a sessile droplet in cylindrical-cap geometry

summary.problem: 2D vapour-diffusion models of evaporating droplets need an arbitrary far-field boundary because of a singularity.
summary.method: Conformal mapping gives an explicit evaporative flux for any contact angle, coupled to internal Stokes flow with an analysis near the contact line.
summary.result: The abstract gives no numbers; it shows the flux diverges at the contact line with the same power law as the 3D spherical-cap case for angles below 90°.

items.why: Closed-form 2D solutions with a contact line at arbitrary angle are rare; one could serve as a verification case for your 2D three-phase contact-line setup.
